content:
Every year a chunk of JEE aspirants lose an easy logarithm mark not because the algebra is hard, but because they forgot that logax is only defined for a > 0, a ≠ 1 and x > 0. Domain first, algebra second — that order is the whole game in this chapter. Logarithm rarely gets a standalone question in JEE Main; instead it hides inside limits, definite integrals, inequalities and complex numbers. Get it wrong early and you carry the error into a five-mark problem.

This is a working guide to the logarithm concepts JEE actually tests, followed by an 8-question online test pitched at real Main and Advanced difficulty. Treat the quiz as a diagnostic: it is not the practice, it tells you where the practice needs to go.

The laws that do the heavy lifting

You already know the three product-quotient-power laws. What JEE checks is whether you apply them without breaking the domain. The classic trap: log(x²) = 2 log x is false in general. It only holds for x > 0. For all real x ≠ 0 you must write log(x²) = 2 log|x|. Drop the modulus and you have quietly halved the domain of your answer.

  • Product: loga(mn) = logam + logan, provided m, n > 0.
  • Power: loga(mp) = p logam — and the modulus caveat above when p is even.
  • Reciprocal of base: logab · logba = 1, a neat check that saves time in Advanced.

Change of base: your most-used tool

Change of base, logab = (logcb) ⁄ (logca), is the single most useful identity in the chapter. It lets you drag every logarithm in a problem to one common base — usually base e or base 10 — so terms actually combine. A frequent Advanced move is substitution: put t = log2x, rewrite the whole equation in t, solve the resulting quadratic, then back-substitute and reject roots that violate x > 0. Miss the rejection step and you gain an extraneous root. Two identities worth keeping on the tip of your tongue for speed: alogax = x, and the base-swap logab = 1 ⁄ logba, which drops straight out of change of base and often saves a full line of working in an Advanced multi-step sum.

The base itself is a variable to watch

When the base contains x — say logx5 — you have two hidden conditions running silently: x > 0 and x ≠ 1. JEE loves setting a problem where the ‘obvious’ answer x = 1 is exactly the value the base forbids.

Log inequalities: where sign errors live

This is the highest-yield trap in the chapter. The rule you must never forget: the direction of a log inequality depends on whether the base is greater than or less than 1.

  • If a > 1, logax is increasing, so logax > logay ⇒ x > y (keep the sign).
  • If 0 < a < 1, logax is decreasing, so logax > logay ⇒ x < y (flip the sign).

In my experience coaching JEE batches, students who write down ‘base > 1 or base < 1?’ in the margin before touching a log inequality make almost no errors here. Those who skip that one line lose the question about half the time. And never forget the invisible constraint: both sides must be positive before you even compare them.

Characteristic and mantissa: the digit-counting question

JEE Main still throws in the occasional common-logarithm (base 10) question about the number of digits or leading zeros. Write log10N as characteristic + mantissa, where the mantissa is the non-negative fractional part in [0, 1).

  • If N ≥ 1 and the characteristic is n, then N has (n + 1) digits before the decimal point.
  • If 0 < N < 1 and the characteristic is −m (written as bar m), there are (m − 1) zeros immediately after the decimal point.

So the number of digits in a big power like 250 is just ⌊50 log102⌋ + 1. With log102 ≈ 0.3010 that is ⌊15.05⌋ + 1 = 16 digits. One formula, one mark, ten seconds.

A realistic plan: one focused day to re-derive every identity yourself (no formula sheet), then two days of mixed inequalities and change-of-base equations, then timed DPP sets so speed becomes automatic. Do the derivations by hand at least once — a formula you can rebuild is a formula you will not misremember under pressure.

quiz.title: Logarithm Online Test for JEE Main & Advanced
quiz.intro: Eight JEE-level questions on log laws, change of base, inequalities, the modulus trap and mantissa. Choose one option per question, then press Check my score and read every solution.

questions.q: If log_2 x + log_2 (x - 2) = 3, then x equals:
questions.explanation: Combine: log_2[x(x-2)] = 3, so x(x-2) = 8, giving x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0, i.e. (x-4)(x+2)=0. x = -2 is rejected (domain needs x > 2), so x = 4.
Write in base 3: log_9 27 = (log_3 27)/(log_3 9) = 3/2. Change of base to a common base is the fastest route.

questions.q: For all real x with x is not 0, log(x^2) equals:
questions.explanation: log(x^2) = 2 log|x| for every non-zero real x. Writing 2 log x silently drops all negative x from the domain. This is the single most common JEE slip.

questions.q: The solution set of log_(0.5)(x) > 2 is:
questions.explanation: Base 0.5 < 1, so log is decreasing and the inequality flips: x < (0.5)^2 = 1/4. With the domain x > 0, the set is 0 < x < 1/4.

questions.q: If log_10 2 is approximately 0.3010, the number of digits in 2^50 is:
The value of log_2 3 . log_3 4 . log_4 5 . log_5 8 is:
questions.explanation: By change of base the chain telescopes to log_2 8 = 3. A product of consecutive-base logs always collapses to log(first base) of the last argument.

questions.q: If log_x 16 = 2, then x equals (x > 0, x is not 1):
questions.explanation: log_x 16 = 2 means x^2 = 16, so x = 4 or x = -4. A logarithm base must be positive and not 1, so x = -4 is rejected. x = 4.

questions.q: The domain of f(x) = log_10 (x - 3) + log_10 (5 - x) is:
questions.explanation: Both arguments must be positive: x - 3 > 0 gives x > 3, and 5 - x > 0 gives x < 5. The domain is the intersection 3 < x < 5.

faq.q: How important is logarithm for JEE Main and Advanced?
faq.a: It rarely appears as a standalone big question, but it is load-bearing: logarithms sit inside limits, definite integrals, inequalities and complex-number problems. A shaky log foundation quietly costs marks across several chapters, so it is worth mastering early even though its direct weightage looks small.

faq.q: What is the most common logarithm mistake JEE students make?
faq.a: Two tie for first. Writing log(x²) = 2 log x instead of 2 log|x|, and forgetting to flip the inequality sign when the base is between 0 and 1. Both come from ignoring the domain and the base condition — check those before you touch the algebra.

faq.q: Do I need to memorise log tables for JEE?
faq.a: No full tables, but keep a few approximate values ready: log<sub>10</sub>2 ≈ 0.3010, log<sub>10</sub>3 ≈ 0.4771 and ln 2 ≈ 0.693. These are enough for digit-counting and quick estimates, and JEE gives you any unusual value you actually need.

faq.q: How do I solve logarithmic equations reliably?
faq.a: Reduce every term to one common base using change of base, substitute the repeated log as a single variable t, solve the resulting polynomial, then back-substitute and reject any root that breaks x > 0 or the base conditions. That last rejection step is where most extraneous-root errors happen.
